item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Iran War Hits Kuwait and Hormuz, Fed Odds Swing, Anthropic's $1.5B Deal
item.description: The Iran war escalates into Kuwait and the Strait of Hormuz as oil surges and Fed hike odds swing. Plus a $1.5 billion Anthropic settlement, a new CFPB lending rule, and Jacksonville's $2 billion budget address.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Tuesday, July 21st. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: The US-Iran war has now spread into Kuwait, with two tankers on fire in the Strait of Hormuz this morning after Iran's tenth straight night under American strikes.

ANDREW: And a federal judge just gave final approval to Anthropic's one point five billion dollar copyright settlement, the largest of its kind in US history. We'll get to what it means for the AI industry.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed at 7,443, down about two tenths of a percent. The Dow fell 307 points, roughly six tenths of a percent, to 51,839. The Nasdaq was nearly flat, down just a twentieth of a percent, at 25,508. It was a quiet, cautious session, with oil prices doing most of the talking. The ten-year Treasury yield sits at 4.59 percent, and the thirty-year fixed mortgage rate is tracking around 6.6 percent according to Mortgage News Daily and the Mortgage Bankers Association. Both are elevated compared to two weeks ago, and both are being pushed by the same thing driving oil this morning.

ANDREW: Let's start there. Iran's war with the United States is now in its tenth straight night, and it's widening. Kuwait says Iranian strikes hit a power and desalination plant over the weekend, the second such attack in two days, and its Mina Al Ahmadi refinery came under drone and missile fire as well. Overnight, two commercial tankers caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz. The Pentagon says nearly 100 US service members have been injured in the last two weeks alone, and at least 17 have died since the fighting resumed in early July, according to a Washington Times tally corroborated by other outlets. The Pentagon has named two of the most recent losses, an Army private and a first lieutenant killed in an attack on a base in Jordan.

JENNY: That's a rough toll for such a short stretch. What's it doing to oil markets?

ANDREW: Brent crude is trading in the high 80s a barrel this morning, still sharply above the mid-70s of two weeks ago, though it's actually eased slightly from Monday's highs near 90. The bigger worry for the region may be water, not just fuel. Kuwait gets ninety percent of its drinking water from desalination, so repeated strikes on that infrastructure are a genuine humanitarian concern, not just an energy story. Iran's Revolutionary Guard also claims to have hit assets in Jordan and Bahrain, and the Houthis in Yemen have separately threatened to blockade Saudi shipping lanes in solidarity, which is exactly the kind of regional spillover the Pentagon has been trying to prevent since this restarted.

JENNY: Is there any diplomatic track left, or is this just escalation for now?

ANDREW: Nothing public. There was a ceasefire memorandum that briefly reopened the strait last month, but Iran's strikes on those commercial vessels broke it, and Trump has called further negotiation a waste of time. Nobody I've seen reporting on this expects a diplomatic off-ramp this week.

ANDREW: All of that is now colliding with the Federal Reserve's calendar. Chair Kevin Warsh and the rest of the committee meet a week from today, on July 28th and 29th, and rate-hike odds for that meeting have been swinging hard along with oil prices, with various market trackers putting the odds anywhere from roughly one in five to nearly one in two over just the past several days. Most economists still expect the Fed to hold next week, but odds of a hike by September, once the oil shock has had more time to feed into inflation data, have climbed well past fifty percent on some trackers. Separately, the Fed's inspector general is still reviewing whether Governor Michelle Bowman broke blackout-period rules by discussing rates at a private Bank of America dinner last month. Warsh told senators questioning him last week that he won't weigh in until that independent review wraps up.

JENNY: So a lot riding on one meeting next week, on top of everything else the committee is dealing with.

ANDREW: More than usual, yes. And that uncertainty is already showing up in home lending, which is where I want to go next. Rates are holding just above six and a half percent. The Mortgage Bankers Association's latest weekly survey put the average thirty-year fixed rate at 6.65 percent, the highest since August of last year, and mortgage applications fell nearly three percent as a result, with purchase applications down seven percent even as refinancing ticked up. Freddie Mac's own weekly survey had it a touch lower, at 6.55 percent, but the direction is the same: rates have risen for two straight weeks as Treasury yields track the Iran-driven oil shock.

JENNY: So anyone hoping to lock in a rate this week is basically fighting geopolitics.

ANDREW: Pretty much. And it's happening against a backdrop of record home prices. HousingWire reports the median existing home sale price hit 440,600 dollars in June, the 36th straight month of year-over-year gains. The Mortgage Bankers Association's data also showed refinancing actually rose four percent even as purchase applications fell, which tells you existing homeowners are still trying to grab whatever relief they can while new buyers increasingly sit on their hands.

ANDREW: The other headline today is regulatory. A new CFPB rule takes effect this morning that eliminates so-called disparate-impact liability under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act's Regulation B. In plain terms, lenders can no longer be held liable simply because a lending practice statistically disadvantages a protected group, unless there's evidence of intentional discrimination.

JENNY: What's the argument for making that change?

ANDREW: Industry groups say the old standard created legal exposure even when there was no intent to discriminate, since almost any lending criterion can produce a statistical disparity somewhere. Consumer advocates counter that disparate-impact liability was one of the few tools regulators had to catch discrimination that isn't obvious or explicit. Worth noting, state fair-lending laws and the federal Fair Housing Act still allow disparate-impact claims, so this doesn't erase the concept everywhere, just under this one federal rule. It's now in effect as of this morning.

JENNY: Worth watching how quickly lenders adjust their compliance playbooks.

ANDREW: Definitely. Jenny, what's the latest on AI?

JENNY: The big AI news actually broke yesterday. A federal judge, Araceli Martínez-Olguín, granted final approval to Anthropic's one point five billion dollar settlement of the class-action copyright suit brought by authors including Andrea Bartz and Charles Graeber. It's the largest copyright class-action settlement in US history. The case centered on claims Anthropic used pirated digital book collections, including Library Genesis, to train Claude. Under the deal, Anthropic pays into a fund for copyright holders and has to destroy the pirated files it downloaded.

ANDREW: Wasn't there already a ruling that training on books was fair use?

JENNY: There was, and that's the interesting wrinkle. Back in 2025, the judge who first oversaw the case found that training an AI model on legally acquired books counts as fair use. Anthropic got in trouble specifically for how it acquired some of the material, not for the training itself. As part of the deal, Anthropic also has to destroy every pirated file it downloaded from sites like Library Genesis. It's becoming the template other AI companies are watching closely: legally sourced training data is probably fine, but shortcuts to get that data are expensive, potentially a billion and a half dollars expensive.

ANDREW: Any sense other publishers or authors might follow with their own suits, now that there's a settlement number on the table?

JENNY: That's the expectation among lawyers covering this. A one and a half billion dollar precedent tends to invite more plaintiffs, not fewer, so this is probably not the last AI copyright settlement we talk about this year.

JENNY: Meanwhile, Google's Gemini 3.5 Pro remains stuck in limited enterprise preview. A widely reported July 17th launch date came and went with no public release, and Bloomberg has reported the delay traces back to Google scrapping and rebuilding parts of the model after it fell short on internal reliability and hallucination testing. There's still no confirmed launch date, no published model card, and no pricing, even though Google first previewed the model back in May.

ANDREW: Two very different AI stories, a huge legal bill on one side and a launch that just won't happen on the other.

JENNY: That's the industry right now. Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at 95 degrees and partly cloudy skies today, with a roughly one-in-four chance of an afternoon storm.

JENNY: Mayor Donna Deegan delivered her budget address to City Council yesterday, proposing a two point oh three billion dollar general fund for the coming fiscal year, about a one percent increase. No property tax rate hike, and notably, no contingency plan built in for November's homestead exemption ballot measure, even though the council auditor has warned that amendment could eventually cost the city over 300 million dollars a year.

ANDREW: That seems like a gamble, banking on voters rejecting it.

JENNY: It's certainly a choice council members are already questioning. About 53 percent of the general fund, just over a billion dollars, goes to public safety, split between the Sheriff's Office and Fire and Rescue. On the capital side, road resurfacing gets a 13 million dollar boost and septic tank phaseout funding jumps by 16 million. Deegan's office says it'll hold eight town halls starting August 5th for public input before the council votes.

JENNY: A couple of other local items. The Planning Commission holds its first public hearing Wednesday on rezoning for the Franklin Arms redevelopment downtown, the project that would demolish the aging complex and replace it with 130 affordable apartments for seniors. Council already approved a one million dollar demolition loan for that project earlier this month.

JENNY: And City Council President Nick Howland's new Financial Audit and Oversight Committee began its 60-day review of JEA's capacity-fee troubles yesterday, even as the city's own inspector general just concluded JEA has been addressing the problem appropriately. Findings from Howland's committee are expected by mid-September.

ANDREW: So JEA gets a partial vote of confidence from one watchdog while another one keeps digging.

JENNY: Right, and it's worth remembering why that fee issue matters. JEA found it had failed to collect capacity fees tied to development expansion for years, due to what the inspector general called data gaps and organizational silos, so this committee is essentially auditing whether that failure cost the city real money.

JENNY: One more, on the infrastructure side. JAXPORT says construction on its new Berth 21 vehicle-handling dock at Blount Island has reached the halfway mark. It's a 60 million dollar project, mostly funded by the state, and it's meant to keep pace with rising auto-import demand through the port. Completion is expected in early 2027.

JENNY: That's Jacksonville for you this week. Back to you, Andrew.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch this week: the Fed's July 28th and 29th meeting. With oil prices elevated and hike odds swinging by the day, the next batch of inflation data due out before then will heavily shape whether Warsh and the committee hold steady or spring a surprise. A hike would be the first of this tightening cycle, and it would ripple straight into mortgage rates already sitting near their highest levels in nearly a year. Keep an eye on the Strait of Hormuz too. If the current spike in tanker attacks continues through the week, oil could push toward triple digits, which would make the Fed's decision even harder and make that mortgage rate even stickier.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Tuesday. Have a great day.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Iran War's Ninth Night, Oil Tops 90 Dollars, Deegan's Budget Address
item.description: The US-Iran war enters a ninth straight night with American casualties rising and oil above 90 dollars a barrel. Plus, Mayor Deegan's budget address, mortgage rates near 6.6 percent, and Google's Gemini delay.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning, and welcome back from the weekend. It's Monday, July 20th. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: The US-Iran war has entered its ninth straight night of strikes, American casualties are mounting, and oil just topped 90 dollars a barrel for the first time in more than a month.

ANDREW: And here in Jacksonville, Mayor Donna Deegan delivers her budget address this morning, just as a new oversight committee opens its inquiry into JEA's finances.

JENNY: We've also got a correction on an AI story we told you about last week, a mortgage market that's still climbing, and a look at what a new federal fair-lending rule changes starting tomorrow.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed Friday at 7,458, down about 1 percent. The Dow fell roughly 400 points, also about 1 percent, to close near 52,146. The Nasdaq dropped 1.4 percent to 25,520. It was the index's first losing week in three, as chip stocks sold off hard and Alphabet shares slid on the Gemini news we'll get to shortly. The ten-year Treasury yield sits at 4.57 percent, and the thirty-year fixed mortgage rate is tracking near 6.6 percent according to Mortgage News Daily. Oil is doing a lot of the driving here, and that's where we start.

ANDREW: Over the weekend, the war between the US and Iran escalated sharply. Iran says the ceasefire has effectively collapsed, and we're now into a ninth consecutive night of strikes.

JENNY: Andrew, what actually changed over the weekend? We'd been tracking six, then seven nights of this a few days ago.

ANDREW: The scope widened. Iranian strikes hit a desalination plant and an oil refinery in Kuwait. A commercial vessel caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz after being struck, and its crew had to abandon ship. On the US side, strikes expanded beyond coastal military sites to roads, tunnels, railways and port infrastructure, including a strike on the city of Tabriz that Iranian media says killed one person and wounded several others.

JENNY: And the American toll?

ANDREW: At least 17 US service members have died since the war resumed, according to a tally reported by the Washington Times and corroborated by CNBC and NPR. That includes two soldiers killed and one still missing after an Iranian missile attack on a US position in Jordan last Friday, and another soldier killed Saturday during a drone incident in northern Iraq. President Trump said overnight that Iran had been hit very hard in retaliation, and CENTCOM says another wave of strikes is already underway this morning. Brent crude is now trading above 90 dollars a barrel, its highest level since mid-June, and that's the direct line to the ten-year yield and mortgage rates we just mentioned.

JENNY: Is there any diplomatic track left, or is it just strikes now?

ANDREW: Officially, talks haven't been declared dead. But practically, nobody is describing anything resembling a truce this morning. The posture on both sides right now is retaliation, not negotiation.

JENNY: What does that mean for people who aren't near the Gulf at all, just watching gas prices here?

ANDREW: It flows through fast. Higher crude means higher pump prices within days, and it pushes up the ten-year Treasury yield, which is the benchmark that mortgage rates track. So a war fought thousands of miles away is already showing up in what it costs to fill your tank and what it costs to buy a house. It's also worth remembering this isn't the first spike we've tracked this month. Oil was trading in the mid-70s just over a week ago, so we're talking about a jump of roughly 15 to 20 percent in a matter of days. We'll get to the mortgage number in a minute, but that's the throughline.

ANDREW: There's a parallel story unfolding at the Federal Reserve. Chair Kevin Warsh faces the Federal Open Market Committee's next meeting on July 28th and 29th, and he's walking into it with a genuine dilemma: does he treat this oil shock as reason to hike, or lean on signs that inflation was already cooling before Iran flared back up. Futures markets now put the odds of a hike somewhere between one-in-five and one-in-three, according to trackers like CME's FedWatch tool, up sharply from just a few weeks ago. Notably, roughly half of the Fed's own policymakers had already penciled in at least one hike this year before this weekend's escalation, so the committee was leaning hawkish even before oil moved.

ANDREW: Warsh is also fielding ethics questions. During his Senate Banking Committee testimony last week, Senator Elizabeth Warren pressed him on Vice Chair Michelle Bowman's attendance at a private Bank of America dinner for Wall Street clients back in June, held during the Fed's blackout period before a rate decision. Warsh said he supports letting the Fed's independent inspector general, Michael Horowitz, review the matter. Bowman maintains she never discussed monetary policy at the dinner, only regulatory topics.

JENNY: So the Fed's credibility and its rate decision are getting litigated in public at the same time.

ANDREW: Exactly the wrong moment for that, with oil prices doing what they're doing.

ANDREW: One more item from Washington worth a mention. Supreme Court Justices Elena Kagan and Amy Coney Barrett testified before a House committee last week, an unusual appearance, asking Congress for close to 230 million dollars in added security funding. Justice Barrett described a swatting incident at her own home. The court says threats against federal judges have topped 370 so far this fiscal year, which tells you something about the temperature of the moment beyond just the war and the Fed.

ANDREW: That oil and rate pressure runs straight into home lending, so let's stay right there. It was a mixed but generally upward week for mortgage rates. Freddie Mac's weekly survey put the thirty-year fixed at 6.55 percent, up from 6.49 percent the week before, the second straight weekly increase. The Mortgage Bankers Association's own survey, for the week ending July 10th, had the average even higher, at 6.65 percent, the highest reading since August of last year. Applications fell 2.7 percent as a result, with purchase applications down 7 percent, though refinancing actually rose 4 percent as some homeowners moved to lock in before rates climb further.

ANDREW: On the regulatory side, a new CFPB rule takes effect tomorrow that eliminates so-called disparate-impact liability from fair lending enforcement under Regulation B. In plain terms, regulators will no longer be able to bring fair-lending cases based purely on statistical outcomes, only on direct evidence of intentional discrimination. Lenders should note that state fair-housing laws still apply, so this doesn't eliminate their exposure entirely, just narrows the federal standard.

ANDREW: Separately, HousingWire has reported that the median home sale price hit a record 440,600 dollars in June, the 36th straight month of gains. And the ROAD to Housing Act, which became law earlier this year, is still waiting on HUD to issue the implementing guidance that would actually put it into effect. Freddie Mac's next weekly rate survey comes out Thursday, and given where oil and yields are sitting this morning, don't expect relief.

ANDREW: Jenny, what's happening in Jacksonville today?

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at mid-90s today with the heat index pushing past 100 degrees, and scattered afternoon storms are likely as the sea breeze kicks in. Forecasters are also watching Tropical Depression Two, which formed in the Gulf over the weekend and is expected to strengthen into Tropical Storm Bertha as it tracks along the northern Gulf Coast. It's not an immediate threat to us, but it's worth keeping an eye on.

JENNY: The big local story today is Mayor Donna Deegan's budget address. She presents her fiscal year twenty twenty-six to twenty-seven budget to City Council this morning at nine, and her office has previewed it as lean, with infrastructure as the top priority. Her office says she'll hold a brief media availability right after, so we should have real numbers to report by this time tomorrow.

ANDREW: Why lean this year specifically?

JENNY: It's largely about the property tax amendment on November's ballot, which would expand the homestead exemption. The city's own Council Auditor estimates that could cost Jacksonville more than 300 million dollars a year in lost revenue by the end of the decade, and that's shaping every budget conversation happening at City Hall right now, including which downtown incentives survive the hearings that follow today's address.

ANDREW: How does the property tax fight change what Council actually cuts?

JENNY: Council President Nick Howland has already flagged downtown incentive packages as the likeliest target once hearings start, since infrastructure and public safety are being protected first. We'll know more once council actually digs into line items over the coming weeks.

JENNY: Separately, a new committee starts its work today too. Howland's Financial Audit and Oversight Committee begins a 60-day review of how JEA failed to collect capacity fees it was owed, with findings due by mid-September. It replaces an earlier investigatory committee that wrapped up in June.

JENNY: One more to flag on the growth front. Four large landowners, including the developer behind Nocatee, have filed fast-tracked development applications under a new state law that lets rural land be developed as intensively as whatever's already built next door, without the standard rezoning process. The largest single parcel is more than 4,400 acres west of the Intracoastal. Separately, a rezoning hearing for the Franklin Arms property is set for Wednesday, and it's worth watching as a test case for how much pushback these fast-tracked applications get at the local level.

JENNY: And we're continuing to follow the investigation into the death of Juan Jairo Coronilla Duran, the 28-year-old killed by a semi-truck last week while fleeing an ICE and Homeland Security Investigations operation on State Road 16 in St. Johns County. The Florida Highway Patrol investigation remains open, with no findings released yet, and community vigils and rallies continued through the weekend.

JENNY: Let's shift to technology, because there's a real correction to make here. Google's Gemini 3.5 Pro, which we'd expected to be widely available by now, is still not out.

ANDREW: Still not out? What happened?

JENNY: Bloomberg reported last week, citing ten current and former Google employees, that the company scrapped and rebuilt the model's base training after it kept falling short on coding performance and reliability. A widely reported July 17th launch target came and went with nothing, and Gemini 3.5 Pro remains limited to a small group of enterprise testers in Vertex AI. Alphabet shares dropped about 4 percent on the news, and prediction markets are now pointing to a release sometime between late July and mid-August.

ANDREW: That's a real opening for competitors.

JENNY: It is, and one place you can see that play out is enterprise finance. Taktile, a startup that builds AI decision-making tools for banks and insurers, just closed a 110 million dollar funding round led by Goldman Sachs Alternatives. Its software is already running underwriting, fraud detection and compliance checks for lenders like Mercury and Monzo, and this round is specifically earmarked to build out more autonomous, agent-based decision-making for regulated financial institutions.

JENNY: It's a reminder that while the frontier labs fight over chatbot benchmarks, a lot of the real money in AI right now is in unglamorous back-office automation.

JENNY: One more to close the loop on. Apple's trade-secrets lawsuit against OpenAI, which we told you about last week, is getting messier. Court filings detail specific allegations against OpenAI's hardware chief, Tang Tan, a 24-year Apple veteran, including that he directed job candidates to bring physical Apple hardware components to interviews and coached departing employees on how to evade Apple's exit security procedures. Apple's suit claims more than 400 former Apple employees now work at OpenAI. OpenAI has denied wrongdoing and says it doesn't need anyone else's trade secrets.

ANDREW: That's a lot of former Apple employees in one building.

JENNY: It is, and it's a big part of why Apple is arguing this is pattern, not coincidence. Apple also names two former employees directly in the suit, along with OpenAI's corporate entities, and is seeking both damages and an injunction. Nobody expects this one to move quickly through the courts, but it's already reshaping how frontier labs think about hiring from rivals.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch over the next ten days: the Fed's July 28th and 29th meeting. Chair Warsh will have to weigh this weekend's oil shock against a June jobs report that came in soft, and he's doing it while an ethics review of his own vice chair plays out in public. Watch whether hike odds keep climbing as oil prices hold above 90 dollars, because that's the number that would ripple fastest into mortgage rates and everything else we've talked about this morning. And closer to home, keep an eye on Freddie Mac's Thursday rate release and whatever Mayor Deegan's budget address actually lands on this morning — both will tell us a lot about how this week shapes up.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Monday. Have a great start to your week.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Sixth Night of Iran Strikes, Fed Odds Tumble, Gemini 3.5 Launches
item.description: The US-Iran war grinds into a sixth night as strikes reach Qatar, Kuwait and Jordan. Fed rate-hike odds collapse after cooler inflation data, mortgage rates tick higher, and Google's Gemini launch collides with Apple's lawsuit against OpenAI.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Friday, July 17th, 2026. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: The US and Iran are now in a sixth straight night of strikes, and overnight the fighting spread further, with Iranian fire reaching Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain and Jordan.

ANDREW: And the odds of a Fed rate hike just fell off a cliff after a surprise inflation reading. Meanwhile, Google launched its newest AI model today, right as Apple's lawsuit against OpenAI gets a lot more specific. We'll get to all of it.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed at 7,533, down about half a percent. The Dow slipped 106 points. The Nasdaq fell nearly one and a half percent, its worst session in weeks, as a sell-off in chip stocks and a drop in Alphabet shares dragged down tech. The ten-year Treasury yield sits just under four point six percent. And the thirty-year fixed mortgage rate is tracking at six point five five percent, according to Freddie Mac's latest weekly survey, up from six point four nine last week. That's the second straight weekly increase, and it traces back directly to the story we're about to get into.

ANDREW: Let's start with the story still driving almost everything else this morning.

ANDREW: The US and Iran are now six consecutive nights into renewed strikes, and this is no longer contained to the two of them. Overnight, Iran fired on American positions in Kuwait and Bahrain, while Jordan and Qatar also came under fire. Iran's health ministry says at least 38 people have been killed inside the country since the strikes resumed this month, and the Pentagon's own toll from Iranian retaliation has climbed into the hundreds wounded.

JENNY: Six nights in a row now — where does that leave the ceasefire talks we've been hearing about all week?

ANDREW: They're alive, barely. Iran's foreign minister is in Muscat this week talking with Oman about a proposal to split the Strait of Hormuz into two shipping corridors — one through Omani waters that stays fully open, one through Iranian waters that would require Tehran's approval but no tolls. The catch is Iran won't commit to it while it's still absorbing nightly strikes, and Washington wants a public guarantee of safe passage before it eases up.

JENNY: And that's part of why oil keeps climbing?

ANDREW: Right. Brent crude is near 85 dollars a barrel, up from 76 just a week ago, and that's flowing straight into Treasury yields and, as we just covered, mortgage rates. The Treasury Department also sanctioned wallets tied to Iran's central bank this week, freezing more than 130 million dollars as part of a broader financial pressure campaign alongside the military one.

ANDREW: Separately, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh wrapped two days of testimony on Capitol Hill this week — a House hearing Tuesday, a tougher Senate session Wednesday where he faced sharp questioning from Senator Elizabeth Warren over ethics concerns involving a Fed colleague. Through both, Warsh gave lawmakers almost nothing on where rates go next. But the bond market answered a different question for him. After Wednesday's producer price report came in cooler than expected, the odds of a rate hike at this month's Fed meeting fell sharply, from over 40 percent earlier in the week to under 20 percent now, according to CME's FedWatch tool.

JENNY: So the inflation data is doing more talking than Warsh is.

ANDREW: For now, yes. Though it's worth noting nine of the eighteen Fed officials have penciled in at least one hike for this year, so the committee itself is more split than the market odds suggest. That yield move is exactly why we're seeing what we're seeing in mortgages.

ANDREW: Freddie Mac's benchmark 30-year fixed rate rose to six point five five percent this week, the second straight weekly increase. The Mortgage Bankers Association's own survey, for the week ending July 10th, had the average even higher, at six point six five percent, the highest reading since last August. Applications fell two point seven percent as a result, with purchase applications down 7 percent, though refinancing actually rose 4 percent as some homeowners moved to lock in before rates climb further.

JENNY: So what does this actually mean for somebody trying to buy a house right now?

ANDREW: It means the math keeps getting tighter. HousingWire reported the median home sale price hit a record 440,600 dollars in June, the 36th straight month of annual gains. Put that next to rates near a one-year high, and affordability is about as stretched as it's been in this cycle. Here's the contrarian detail, though: a year ago this week, Freddie Mac's average was six point seven five percent. So as painful as this run-up feels, buyers today are technically still getting a slightly better rate than they were twelve months ago.

ANDREW: Two regulatory items worth flagging. A new CFPB rule takes effect next Tuesday, July 21st, pulling back the agency's disparate-impact enforcement approach to fair lending — lenders and consumer advocates are both watching how examiners apply it in practice. And the ROAD to Housing Act, which became law earlier this year, is still waiting on HUD to issue actual implementation guidance, so its real-world effect on buyers remains an open question for now.

ANDREW: Jenny, over to you. I hear there's a big AI headline today.

JENNY: There is. Google's Gemini three point five Pro went fully available to the public today, and the timing isn't an accident. It's landing the same day as the World AI Conference, which people in the industry are already calling the biggest AI news day of the year.

ANDREW: What's actually different about this one?

JENNY: The headline feature is a two-million-token context window, so it can hold roughly a full novel's worth of material in a single conversation. There's also a new Deep Think reasoning mode, though that's locked behind Google's 250-dollar-a-month Ultra tier. On the developer side, Google priced the API at a dollar twenty-five per million input tokens and 10 dollars per million output tokens, competitive with what Anthropic and OpenAI charge for their top models.

ANDREW: How's that landing against the competition?

JENNY: It's squarely aimed at enterprise customers who've been asking for bigger context windows to handle entire codebases or document sets at once. Anthropic, for context, is still holding its own — its annualized revenue run rate is near 47 billion dollars, and the company says it expects to be profitable this year, ahead of OpenAI. OpenAI, meanwhile, just shipped its own agentic product, ChatGPT Work, folding its Codex coding tool into the desktop app.

JENNY: Meanwhile, the Apple versus OpenAI lawsuit we told you about is getting a lot more specific. Apple's complaint now names OpenAI's hardware chief, Tang Tan, a former Apple vice president, accusing him of directing OpenAI job candidates to bring, quote, actual parts from Apple to their interviews. Apple also alleges a separate OpenAI employee downloaded dozens of confidential files on unreleased Apple hardware. OpenAI's spokesperson says the company has no interest in other companies' trade secrets.

ANDREW: That's a pretty vivid allegation for a corporate lawsuit.

JENNY: It is, and it's a reminder of how personal the fight for AI hardware talent has become between two companies that used to just compete on software.

JENNY: One quick data point on safety, since it doesn't get as much airtime as the product launches. The Future of Life Institute released its 2026 AI Safety Index this week, and Anthropic earned the highest grade in the industry, a C-plus, with OpenAI and Google DeepMind close behind at a C. For an industry moving this fast, even the leader getting a C-plus tells you something about how early we still are.

JENNY: One more from the frontier labs. Anthropic is in early talks with Samsung about building a custom AI chip on Samsung's advanced 2-nanometer process. Nothing's signed, and Anthropic is reportedly still talking to multiple chipmakers, but Samsung already has skin in the game. It was part of Anthropic's 65-billion-dollar funding round back in May, alongside SK Hynix and Micron.

JENNY: Let's bring it home to Jacksonville.

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at a high near 93 today, with a heat index around 102 and a decent chance of afternoon thunderstorms.

JENNY: The story we've been following since Tuesday out of St. Johns County has a few updates. A 28-year-old Mexican national died after fleeing a Homeland Security Investigations and ICE operation at a gas station on State Road 16, running into the path of a tractor-trailer. The driver stopped and tried to help, but the man died at the scene.

ANDREW: Has anyone said what led to the stop in the first place?

JENNY: Not yet. Florida Highway Patrol is still investigating the crash itself, DHS has confirmed the operation happened but hasn't detailed what prompted it, and community vigils have continued through the week. It's now the third death connected to an ICE encounter nationwide in the past week, following incidents in Houston and Maine.

JENNY: Closer to City Hall, a new committee starts work Monday. The Financial Audit and Oversight Committee takes over from the council's old JEA investigative panel, with a 60-day clock to dig into how JEA failed to collect capacity fees from large customers like Mayo Clinic. That same day, Mayor Donna Deegan delivers her budget address, which she's already previewing as lean, with infrastructure as the top spending priority — and this year's budget fight is shadowed by a November ballot measure that could cost the city over 300 million dollars a year in property tax revenue by the end of the decade.

ANDREW: Two big Monday storylines to watch, then.

JENNY: Exactly. There's also a land story worth watching. Four large landowners, including Nocatee's developer, filed fast-tracked development applications within hours of a new state law taking effect that lets rural land be developed as intensively as whatever's next door, without the usual county rezoning process. The largest single parcel is more than 4,400 acres west of the Intracoastal.

ANDREW: That's a lot of land moving fast.

JENNY: It is, and it's exactly the kind of thing that'll come up again once people see what actually gets built. And overnight, JSO is investigating a fatal shooting on Broward Road on the Northside, where a man in his twenties or thirties was found with a gunshot wound and later died at the hospital. No arrests yet.

JENNY: On a lighter note, downtown's momentum keeps building. The completion of One Tower Court in the Shipyards district is being read locally as proof that the riverfront redevelopment around the new Four Seasons is actually taking hold, not just sitting on paper.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch: the Fed's next meeting, July 28th and 29th. It's the first time Chair Warsh has to weigh a real oil shock against a labor market that just delivered a stunningly weak jobs report, only 57,000 jobs added in June, well below forecasts, alongside a downward revision to May's count as well. Markets are currently pricing less than a 20 percent chance of a hike, but with oil near 85 dollars a barrel and the Iran war showing no sign of slowing, that number could move fast in either direction. Watch the CME FedWatch odds between now and next Tuesday's CFPB rule change — both land in the same stretch of days and both will shape what borrowing costs look like heading into fall.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Friday. Have a great weekend.

ANDREW: We'll see you Monday.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Iran Strikes Widen, Warsh Wraps Senate Testimony, Anthropic Launches Ode
item.description: US strikes hit Iran again overnight as Tehran retaliates across the Gulf. Fed Chair Warsh wraps two days of testimony without tipping his hand. Anthropic and Blackstone launch a billion and a half dollar AI venture, and mortgage rates ease off a multi-month high.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Thursday, July 16th. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: The US military launched another wave of strikes on Iran overnight, and Tehran hit back at American bases in three different countries. We'll get into just how dangerous this is getting.

ANDREW: And in AI, Anthropic just launched a billion and a half dollar venture with Blackstone and Goldman Sachs, betting on something bigger than the models themselves.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed at 7,572, up about four tenths of a percent. The Dow added 150 points to close near 52,659. The Nasdaq climbed six tenths of a percent to just over 26,269, with Apple hitting a new all-time high after a cooler than expected wholesale inflation report. The ten-year Treasury yield sits around 4.57 percent, and the thirty-year fixed mortgage rate is tracking at 6.64 percent according to Mortgage News Daily, down a touch today but still near the highest levels since last summer. We'll get into why in a few minutes.

ANDREW: Let's start with Iran, because the situation escalated again overnight.

ANDREW: US Central Command launched a fresh round of strikes early this morning, hitting Iranian command centers, air defense sites, and coastal surveillance facilities on Qeshm Island, near Bandar Abbas, and at Chabahar. The stated goal is degrading Iran's ability to threaten shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

JENNY: And Iran struck back?

ANDREW: It did. Tehran says it hit American military assets in Kuwait, Bahrain, and Jordan with missiles and drones, including Patriot missile batteries and fuel depots at Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait. Iran's health ministry says at least 35 people were killed and more than 300 wounded in the most recent round of American strikes. On the US side, the Pentagon's death toll for troops now stands at 14, with more than 400 wounded, after a Navy helicopter pilot was killed earlier this month.

JENNY: This is happening less than a month after the two sides signed that ceasefire extension.

ANDREW: Right, and that's the story here. That memorandum of understanding from June is essentially dead in practice, with both sides now accusing each other of violating it. Iran's military is also warning it will, in its words, crush regional infrastructure if the US strikes civilian sites. Oil is the transmission mechanism to watch. Brent crude is still elevated near 85 dollars a barrel, and that's a big reason Treasury yields and mortgage rates haven't come down the way cooling inflation data would normally suggest.

JENNY: Is there any diplomatic progress at all in the middle of this?

ANDREW: A little. As we've been tracking, Oman has been pushing a two-corridor plan for the Strait of Hormuz. Ships would move freely through a southern corridor in Omani waters, while a northern corridor in Iranian waters would require Tehran's permission but no tolls. Iran's foreign minister and Oman's foreign minister discussed the mechanics of it again this week. The holdup is that Washington wants Iran to publicly guarantee safe passage and drop any toll plan before it eases the blockade, and Iran hasn't been willing to commit to that while it's still absorbing strikes.

JENNY: So the diplomacy is running on a completely different clock than the fighting.

ANDREW: That's a fair way to put it.

ANDREW: Meanwhile, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh wrapped two days of testimony on Capitol Hill, appearing before the Senate Banking Committee yesterday after his House appearance a day earlier. He didn't give lawmakers much of a signal on where rates are headed next, but he was direct on inflation, telling senators the Fed has, quote, no tolerance for persistently elevated inflation. He also touched on bank capital rules, guardrails around digital assets, and safety protocols for AI in the financial system.

JENNY: So no real hint on the September meeting?

ANDREW: Not really, and that's actually notable, because heading into this week, odds of another hike had cooled toward 45 percent on the back of that soft June inflation report. This oil shock complicates the picture, and Warsh seemed to be deliberately keeping his options open.

ANDREW: One more from Washington. Supreme Court Justices Elena Kagan and Amy Coney Barrett made a rare appearance before Congress this week, testifying about a rise in threats against federal judges and asking for more security funding. Justice Barrett told lawmakers she once had to wear a bulletproof vest home from the court, and struggled to explain that to her twelve year old son.

JENNY: That's a striking image. Andrew, let's get to what all of this means for mortgage rates.

ANDREW: So here's the direct line from Tehran to your mortgage rate.

ANDREW: The thirty-year fixed hit 6.75 percent on Mortgage News Daily's index earlier this week, the highest since late July of last year, before easing back to 6.64 percent today on that cooler producer price report. The Mortgage Bankers Association's own weekly survey, covering the week ending July 10th, put the average even higher, at 6.65 percent, also the highest since last August.

JENNY: So which is it? Are rates going up or down?

ANDREW: Both, in a sense. The trend since the Iran conflict flared back up has clearly been higher, because oil-driven inflation risk is keeping Treasury yields elevated even as core inflation data cools. Today's dip just reflects one good data point pushing back against that pressure. Freddie Mac's own weekly survey updates today too. Its last reading, from July 9th, had the thirty-year at 6.49 percent, so watch whether that number moves up toward where the daily indexes already sit.

ANDREW: On volume, the Mortgage Bankers Association says overall applications fell two and a half percent last week, driven by a seven percent drop in purchase applications, even as refinancing ticked up. HousingWire also flagged that the median home sale price hit a record 440,600 dollars in June, the thirty sixth straight month of gains, so buyers are getting squeezed from both the rate side and the price side.

JENNY: Rough combination.

ANDREW: It is. One more to flag. A new CFPB rule scaling back fair-lending disparate-impact enforcement takes effect next Tuesday, July 21st. Worth watching how lenders respond. And on the regulatory side, the ROAD to Housing Act is now law, but HUD still hasn't issued implementation guidance, so lenders are largely waiting on the sidelines for details on how it'll actually work in practice.

ANDREW: Jenny, let's turn to something that has nothing to do with Iran or the Fed for once. AI.

JENNY: Gladly. The big story is a new company called Ode.

JENNY: Anthropic teamed up with Blackstone, Hellman and Friedman, Goldman Sachs, and a handful of other investors to launch a billion and a half dollar joint venture focused on actually implementing AI inside big companies, not building new models.

ANDREW: Wait, a billion and a half dollars just to help companies use AI that already exists?

JENNY: Basically, yes. Anthropic, Blackstone, and Hellman and Friedman reportedly put in around 300 million dollars each, Goldman kicked in roughly 150 million, and firms like General Atlantic, Apollo, and Sequoia rounded out the rest. Ode launched with about 100 engineers who'll embed directly inside enterprise customers and rebuild their workflows around Claude specifically. The bet is that deploying AI well is going to be a bigger business than the models themselves.

ANDREW: That's a real vote of confidence from some serious money managers.

JENNY: It is, and it mirrors a similar move from OpenAI, which is chasing the same enterprise deployment opportunity. Speaking of OpenAI, its lawsuit with Apple took an odd turn this week. Apple's trade-secrets case alleges OpenAI's hardware chief directed departing Apple employees to bring actual parts into job interviews for what Apple's complaint calls show and tell. OpenAI now says it actually did respond to Apple's early complaints, and that settlement talks broke down over what amounts to a lawyer's email mix-up.

ANDREW: An email mix-up derailing a corporate lawsuit. That's very 2026.

JENNY: It really is. And on the model front, Microsoft has now made OpenAI's newest model, GPT 5.6, the default in Microsoft 365 Copilot, so if you use Copilot at work, you're likely already running on it.

ANDREW: Any update on where Anthropic's own numbers stand?

JENNY: Anthropic says its annualized revenue run rate is now around 47 billion dollars, and the company maintains it's on track to turn profitable well ahead of OpenAI. It's also worth remembering Apple confirmed the new Siri will run on Google's Gemini, not any OpenAI model, so this fight over who powers the next generation of AI products is playing out on several fronts at once, not just in court.

JENNY: Let's bring it home to Jacksonville.

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at the low nineties today with a heat index near 100 and a chance of afternoon sea breeze storms. Forecasters are also watching a system over the Gulf with about a 20 percent chance of tropical development this weekend.

JENNY: The biggest local story right now is a tragedy in neighboring St. Johns County. A 28 year old man died Tuesday morning after running from an encounter with ICE and Homeland Security Investigations agents at a gas station on State Road 16, into the path of a semi-truck. The Florida Highway Patrol is investigating.

ANDREW: How has the community responded?

JENNY: With real grief and real anger. A crowd gathered Wednesday night at the crash site with candles, flowers, and signs, and advocates are planning a rally in Jacksonville. DHS confirmed the operation but hasn't released details on what led to it. The Florida Highway Patrol says the man was a Mexican national, and the investigation is ongoing.

JENNY: Closer to City Hall, Jacksonville's new Financial Audit and Oversight Committee starts work Monday, July 20th. It's a narrower successor to the JEA committee that expired in June without a final report, and it has just 60 days, until September 18th, to figure out how JEA failed to collect capacity fees from major customers like Mayo Clinic, and recommend fixes.

ANDREW: Any sense of how much money we're talking about?

JENNY: The city's Inspector General has said the failures trace back to data gaps, old record transitions, and organizational breakdowns rather than any one bad actor, but the exact dollar figure is still part of what this committee is supposed to nail down.

ANDREW: Didn't Moody's just weigh in on JEA too?

JENNY: They did, a few weeks back. Moody's upgraded JEA's electric bonds, citing governance progress under the utility's reconstituted board, but the agency warned that continued political turmoil or more leadership churn could put that upgrade at risk. So this new committee's conduct over the next 60 days actually matters for JEA's borrowing costs, not just its reputation.

JENNY: And one to watch on the growth side. The Jacksonville Business Journal reports four large landowners, including the developer behind Nocatee, applied for fast-tracked development within hours of a new state law taking effect that lets rural land be developed as intensively as neighboring parcels, without the usual county rezoning process. The biggest parcel is more than 4,400 acres west of the Intracoastal.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch this week. The Fed's next move isn't until the July 28th and 29th meeting, but keep an eye on how Chair Warsh talks about oil and inflation in the coming days. He walked out of two days of testimony without tipping his hand, and with Brent crude still elevated near 85 dollars a barrel, the case for a September hike could firm back up fast if energy prices keep climbing.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Thursday. Have a great day.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Cooling CPI Collides With Iran Blockade as Warsh Faces Senate
item.description: June inflation cooled sharply, but an intensifying Iran blockade keeps oil and mortgage rates elevated ahead of Fed Chair Warsh's first Senate testimony. Plus JEA's oversight shake-up, Apple versus OpenAI escalates, and Anthropic's next move.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Wednesday, July 15th. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: Overnight, the US and Iran traded another round of strikes, and Iran's health ministry says more than 260 people were wounded as the reinstated blockade on Iranian ports takes full effect.

ANDREW: And on a very different front, Apple's trade-secrets lawsuit against OpenAI got sharper overnight, with OpenAI firing back that it sees no evidence the complaint has merit.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed at seven thousand five hundred forty three Tuesday, up about four tenths of a percent. The Dow was basically flat, up just a few points to fifty two thousand five hundred eight. The Nasdaq led again, up nearly one percent to twenty six thousand one hundred seven, as chip stocks rallied on a much cooler than expected inflation report. Here's the strange part, though. The ten-year Treasury yield barely moved, still sitting near four point six two percent, close to a two-month high. Normally, cooler inflation sends yields lower. Not this week. The Iran-driven oil spike is pulling in the opposite direction. And the thirty-year fixed mortgage rate is tracking right around six point six percent, according to Mortgage News Daily, essentially unchanged from Tuesday for that same reason.

ANDREW: Let's start with why that tug of war is happening in the first place.

ANDREW: Yesterday's inflation report was a genuine surprise. June consumer prices actually fell four tenths of a percent for the month, pulling the annual rate down to three and a half percent, well below the three point eight percent economists expected, and down sharply from May's four point two. Core inflation, which strips out food and energy, was flat on the month and now sits at two point six percent a year.

JENNY: That's a big miss. What's driving it?

ANDREW: Falling gas prices, mostly. Energy costs dropped nearly six percent in June. But that number is already stale. Since the ceasefire fell apart, oil is up more than fifteen percent this month alone, so July's report is unlikely to look nearly this good.

JENNY: Which brings us to what's happening in the Gulf right now.

ANDREW: Right. The blockade the President announced Monday is now fully in effect, and overnight the US carried out another wave of strikes, hitting dozens of targets over about seven hours. Iran's health ministry says more than 260 people were wounded, the highest single-night toll since the strikes resumed. Bahrain and Kuwait both had missile-alert sirens go off again early this morning.

JENNY: And Iran's answering by going after the oil supply itself?

ANDREW: Its Revolutionary Guard is now threatening to shut down additional energy export routes across the region, not just the strait. Shipping data from the firm Kpler shows only seventeen vessels transited Hormuz on Monday. Traffic has essentially stalled. Brent crude is near eighty five dollars a barrel, WTI near eighty, and that's the pressure keeping yields and mortgage rates elevated even as the inflation data cools.

ANDREW: There is one thread of actual diplomacy in here. Iran's foreign minister met his Omani counterpart in Muscat over the weekend, and Oman has floated a plan to split the strait into two lanes, a southern corridor through Omani waters that would stay fully open, and a northern corridor through Iranian waters that would require Iran's advance approval. The two sides agreed to keep talking, but Washington is still demanding Iran commit to zero tolls and zero attacks before it will even consider easing the blockade.

ANDREW: All of which lands on new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's desk at the worst possible moment. He told the House yesterday that a cooler CPI print is not, quote, mission accomplished, and that the Fed has no tolerance for persistently elevated inflation. He also rolled out five new task forces to study everything from the Fed's communications to its balance sheet, and when asked directly if he works for the President, he said, quote, we're an independent central bank, we're honored to be independent. He testifies before the Senate Banking Committee this morning at ten Eastern, his first appearance there since taking over in May.

JENNY: Anything else notable out of yesterday's session?

ANDREW: One line stuck with me. Asked about the economy more broadly, Warsh said it seems inevitable that what people are calling, quote, AI investment will soon just be called investment, meaning it's becoming so central to growth that the Fed can't treat it as a side story anymore. Given how much of this broadcast is about AI most mornings, that's a Fed chair basically agreeing with our rundown.

JENNY: So does the cooler inflation number give him room to sound less hawkish today?

ANDREW: That's exactly the tension senators will be probing. Odds of a rate hike at the September meeting had cooled to somewhere around forty five percent right after yesterday's CPI report, down from well over sixty just a day earlier. Whether that number holds or climbs back up may depend less on what Warsh says this morning than on what happens next in the Gulf.

JENNY: Let's follow that thread into what it means for anyone trying to buy or refinance right now. Andrew?

ANDREW: It's a strange moment for mortgage rates. Normally, a CPI report that good would send rates lower fast. Instead, the thirty-year fixed is holding right around six point six percent, barely budged from Tuesday, because the bond market is more focused on oil than on that one inflation print.

JENNY: So the good inflation news basically got canceled out?

ANDREW: Almost exactly canceled out. Freddie Mac's official weekly survey comes out tomorrow, and that'll be the next real read on where things stand. Its last print, a week ago Thursday, had the rate at six point four nine percent, so we're already tracking meaningfully higher than that.

ANDREW: Two other threads still worth watching on this beat. The ROAD to Housing Act, the biggest federal housing law since 1990, is now on the books, but HUD still hasn't issued the guidance lenders need on how the new limits on large institutional investors will actually work. And a new CFPB rule scaling back fair-lending enforcement takes effect a week from today.

JENNY: Any sense of how buyers are handling rates this high?

ANDREW: They're stretched. HousingWire's June numbers put the median home sale price at a record four hundred forty thousand six hundred dollars, the thirty-sixth straight month of gains. Add a six point six percent rate on top of record prices, and affordability is being squeezed from both directions at once.

ANDREW: Jenny, switch gears with me. You've got real drama on the AI beat today.

JENNY: I do. Apple's trade-secrets lawsuit against OpenAI got a real response overnight. OpenAI said, quote, we're not aware of any evidence that this complaint has merit, which is a sharper denial than the vague statement they put out Monday.

ANDREW: Remind me what Apple's actually alleging again.

JENNY: That OpenAI's hardware chief, a twenty four year Apple veteran named Tang Tan, ran a recruiting campaign built around Apple's own confidential project code names, and that a former Apple engineer who joined OpenAI kept his Apple laptop after leaving and pulled files off of it. Apple says this was deliberate, not a few rogue hires, and that it flagged the concerns to OpenAI back in February and got nowhere.

ANDREW: That's a serious allegation to make about a company's culture, not just its people.

JENNY: It is, and it's a sharp reversal for two companies that were still partnered on Apple Intelligence not that long ago. Worth noting, Apple has also confirmed the new Siri will run on Google's Gemini instead of any OpenAI model, so this relationship is clearly over on more than one front.

JENNY: The other story on this beat: Anthropic's business keeps accelerating. New reporting puts its annualized revenue run rate near forty seven billion dollars, up from the forty five billion figure we mentioned yesterday, and the company says it's on track to be profitable this year, largely on the strength of Claude Code and enterprise adoption.

ANDREW: Forty seven billion, revised up in a single day? That's a fast-moving number.

JENNY: It is, and Anthropic is also in talks with Samsung to help build its first custom AI chip, using Samsung's newest two nanometer manufacturing process, according to The Information. It's early. No actual chip design has started yet. But it's a sign of how much these companies want to control their own compute costs instead of renting all of it from Nvidia.

ANDREW: Worth watching whether that chip talk turns into an actual deal.

JENNY: Definitely. Alright, let's bring it back home to Jacksonville.

JENNY: Weather-wise, it's going to be a hot one. Sunshine gives way to building clouds this afternoon, highs in the low nineties, but the heat index will feel close to a hundred degrees. A weak sea breeze could spark a few isolated storms later on, so don't expect rain everywhere, but if it hits your neighborhood, expect it to come down hard.

JENNY: And actually, that Iran story we opened with is already showing up at the pump here. Florida gas prices jumped twelve cents overnight, according to AAA, with the Jacksonville-area average now at three dollars and ninety cents a gallon.

ANDREW: So the Gulf story reaches all the way to the corner gas station.

JENNY: Exactly. On the local government side, there's a real shift happening in the JEA oversight fight. City Council's original special investigatory committee, the one Ron Salem has been chairing, expired at the end of June without a final findings report. In its place, a new Financial Audit and Oversight Committee starts up July 20th, running sixty days, narrowly focused on the millions of dollars in capacity fees JEA never collected from big customers like the Mayo Clinic.

ANDREW: Didn't Moody's just weigh in on JEA's finances too?

JENNY: They did, a few weeks back. Moody's actually upgraded JEA's electric bonds, crediting stronger finances and governance progress under the utility's reconstituted board. But the agency was blunt that continued political turmoil or leadership churn could send that rating right back down, so this new committee's work carries real weight for JEA's borrowing costs, not just its politics.

JENNY: On a lighter note, JEA is hosting its monthly Senior Day resource fair today at its downtown headquarters, with the Jacksonville Public Library joining as a new partner this month, plus free water-efficiency kits for anyone who stops by.

ANDREW: Nice contrast to everything else going on inside that building.

JENNY: It is. And one more to flag, the Sheriff's Office town hall series keeps rolling. Sheriff T. K. Waters has been getting pointed questions at each stop about the JSO budget and teen crime, with two district meetings left before the series wraps on July 23rd. That same week, the Planning Commission takes up the Franklin Arms rezoning, which would clear the way for a fifty million dollar senior housing project.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch today: Kevin Warsh's testimony before the Senate Banking Committee at ten a.m. Eastern. It's his first appearance there since taking over the Fed, and it comes less than twenty four hours after a cooler than expected inflation report ran headlong into a fresh oil shock out of the Gulf. Watch whether he leans on that CPI number to sound calmer than he did in the House yesterday, or whether the renewed blockade and Iran's threats against regional energy routes keep him just as guarded. His tone this morning will say a lot about whether that September rate hike is really back in play.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Wednesday. Have a great day.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Iran Blockade Jolts Oil and Markets as CPI, Warsh Testimony Loom
item.description: Trump reinstates an Iran blockade and slaps a 20 percent Hormuz shipping fee, rattling markets hours before June's inflation report and Fed Chair Warsh's first Hill testimony. Plus mortgage rates climb, Anthropic overtakes OpenAI in revenue, and Jacksonville's sheriff town halls continue.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Tuesday, July 14th. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: Overnight, President Trump reinstated a blockade on Iranian ports and slapped a 20 percent fee on any cargo moving through the Strait of Hormuz. Oil jumped again this morning, and the ceasefire from last month looks all but finished.

ANDREW: And in Washington, new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh makes his first appearance before Congress this morning, just hours after the government releases the June inflation report.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed at seven thousand five hundred fifteen Monday, down about eight tenths of a percent. The Dow slipped a quarter percent to fifty two thousand four hundred ninety eight. The Nasdaq took the hardest hit, down about one and a half percent to twenty five thousand eight hundred seventy three, as chip and tech names led the retreat. The ten-year Treasury yield is trading near four point six percent, close to a two-month high. And the thirty-year fixed mortgage rate is tracking at six point seven two percent as of Monday, according to Mortgage News Daily, up noticeably from last week as oil and yields climb together. Energy shares were about the only bright spot in an otherwise rough session.

ANDREW: Let's start with what's driving all of it.

ANDREW: Overnight, the President announced the US is reinstating a full blockade of Iranian ports near the Strait of Hormuz, and as of four p.m. Eastern yesterday, the US began charging a 20 percent fee on any cargo shipped through the strait. It's the clearest signal yet that last month's ceasefire is dead. Iran's Revolutionary Guard hit a container ship in the strait over the weekend, and the US answered with its third round of strikes in a week, hitting more than a hundred forty military targets.

JENNY: Wait, the US is charging a fee just to use the strait? What's the thinking there?

ANDREW: Part economic pressure, part revenue play. Washington is framing it as the cost of keeping the strait open, and it's designed to squeeze anyone still doing business with Tehran. But the number markets actually care about is crude. WTI is back above eighty dollars a barrel, Brent is near eighty seven, and shipping traffic through Hormuz has all but stopped this week.

JENNY: And that's the strait that carries something like a fifth of the world's oil.

ANDREW: Right, which is why oil, yields, and the dollar are all moving together this morning. And it's not staying contained to the strait itself. Iran hit back at American allies over the weekend, missile and drone attacks on sites tied to US forces in Bahrain, Kuwait, and Jordan. Bahrain, which hosts the Navy's Fifth Fleet, had missile-alert sirens going off again as recently as this morning.

JENNY: So this is spreading regionally, not just staying a shipping story.

ANDREW: It is, though there's one thread of good news buried in all of it. Iran's foreign minister met his Omani counterpart in Muscat over the weekend on safe-passage talks. So even with strikes happening nightly, there's still a diplomatic channel open. The White House, for its part, has called negotiating with Iran right now a waste of time, so nobody should expect that channel to produce anything fast.

ANDREW: All of that is landing on the worst possible day for the Fed. The Labor Department releases the June inflation report at eight-thirty this morning, with economists expecting the headline rate to ease to around three point nine percent, largely because gas prices fell before this latest flare-up. Core inflation, which strips out food and energy, is expected to hold stubbornly near two point nine percent.

JENNY: So today's the day Chair Warsh finally has to face Congress.

ANDREW: His first appearance since taking over the Fed in May. He testifies before the House Financial Services Committee this morning, then the Senate Banking Committee tomorrow. He's stayed tight-lipped on where rates are headed through his first seven weeks, but with oil spiking again right as he's expected to sound reassuring on inflation, lawmakers are going to press him hard on whether the war changes his timeline.

JENNY: What else are lawmakers likely to grill him on?

ANDREW: Expect questions on the Fed's balance sheet plans too, separate from rates. But the headline fight will be inflation versus geopolitics. A Fed chair who's spent seven weeks refusing to commit to a path now has to explain that path in person, on camera, on the same morning oil is spiking.

ANDREW: One more national story to close the loop on. South Carolina's Senate vacancy has been filled. Governor Henry McMaster appointed Darline Graham Nordone, the late Senator Lindsey Graham's sister, to serve out his term, after President Trump publicly recommended her as, quote, a fabulous tribute to Lindsey. She'll be sworn in as South Carolina's first female senator. It's an interim posting only. Candidates get a one-week filing window starting July 21st, ahead of an August 11th special primary for the remaining four years of the term.

JENNY: A family stepping into the seat right as the filing clock starts.

JENNY: Let's follow the money from the geopolitics into people's wallets. Andrew, what's happening with mortgage rates?

ANDREW: It's the same story, just showing up in a different market. Mortgage News Daily has the thirty-year fixed at six point seven two percent, up from six point four nine on last week's Freddie Mac survey, which was already the highest weekly read since spring.

JENNY: So the Fed hasn't even acted, and rates are moving anyway?

ANDREW: Exactly. This is the bond market pricing in more persistent inflation risk because of the oil shock, not anything Warsh has said or done. If oil keeps climbing, the ten-year yield follows, and mortgage rates move within days.

ANDREW: The other story we're still tracking: the ROAD to Housing Act, the biggest piece of federal housing legislation since 1990, officially became law over the weekend without Trump's signature. He let it pass without a veto despite a separate fight with Congress over voter ID. Its key provision restricts large institutional investors, ones who already own more than 350 single-family homes, from buying more outside of new rental construction.

JENNY: How is the industry reacting?

ANDREW: Still early. HUD hasn't issued implementation guidance yet, so lenders and investors are mostly in wait-and-see mode. Also on the calendar, a new CFPB rule pulling back fair-lending enforcement takes effect a week from today, July 21st.

JENNY: With rates this high, is anyone actually still buying?

ANDREW: Some, but it's getting more expensive. HousingWire put the median home sale price at a record four hundred forty thousand six hundred dollars in June, up almost two percent from a year ago. That's the thirty-sixth straight month prices have risen. Combine record prices with rates pushing back toward six and three quarters, and affordability is getting squeezed from both directions at once.

ANDREW: Jenny, you've got a wild one on the AI beat.

JENNY: I do. Apple's lawsuit against OpenAI over trade secrets got messier. OpenAI broke its silence with a statement saying, quote, we have no interest in other companies' trade secrets. It doesn't really address what's in the complaint.

ANDREW: Remind me what Apple's actually alleging.

JENNY: That OpenAI's hardware chief, a 24-year Apple veteran named Tang Tan, ran a recruiting campaign that leaned on Apple's own confidential project code names, coached departing employees on how to dodge Apple's security checks, and that one of those employees kept his Apple laptop after leaving and pulled confidential documents off of it. Apple says it flagged this to OpenAI back in February and got no response before filing suit.

ANDREW: So this isn't just leftover tension from the old ChatGPT-iPhone partnership. It's a real trade-secrets claim.

JENNY: Right, and it's a sharp reversal for two companies that were partners on the iPhone just two years ago.

JENNY: The other big AI story this week: Anthropic has pulled ahead of OpenAI in revenue for the first time. The Information reports Anthropic's annualized run rate is now around forty five billion dollars, versus roughly thirty three billion for OpenAI, a reflection of Anthropic's enterprise and coding bet paying off faster than OpenAI's consumer-heavy business.

ANDREW: That's a real reversal of the pecking order.

JENNY: It is, and it's worth watching whether that gap holds up as more numbers come in, especially since enterprise AI adoption keeps outpacing the governance rules companies have in place to manage it. Surveys are showing more than half of financial firms now using agentic AI in some form, but a lot of them are still figuring out how to keep those agents from overstepping what they're supposed to do.

ANDREW: That gap between adoption and control seems like the real story underneath the revenue numbers.

JENNY: It is. The models aren't the bottleneck anymore. Trust in them is.

ANDREW: Alright, let's bring it back local. Jenny, what's happening in Jacksonville?

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at a high of 88 today, partly cloudy with a decent shot of afternoon storms, about a 50 percent chance, so keep the umbrella handy if you're headed out this afternoon.

JENNY: On the local beat, the Sheriff's Office continues its six-district town hall tour tonight. District 3 gets its turn at Church of Eleven22's Mandarin campus.

ANDREW: How's that series gone so far?

JENNY: It kicked off in District 5 yesterday and runs through July 23rd. Sheriff T. K. Waters is using it to update residents on public safety initiatives and take questions directly from the community, and residents can even submit questions in advance by email.

JENNY: Also this week, JEA holds its monthly Senior Day resource fair tomorrow at its downtown headquarters, free help with utility bills and water efficiency kits, with the Jacksonville Public Library joining as a new partner this month.

ANDREW: Nice bit of counter-programming to the bigger oversight questions still hanging over JEA.

JENNY: Definitely, and on that front, we're still waiting on Mayor Deegan's budget address, which comes to City Council a week from Monday, on July 20th. That's expected to be the moment we learn which downtown incentives survive given the pressure from November's property tax amendment on the ballot.

ANDREW: Anything new on the Massey Contracting case?

JENNY: No real movement to report. The owner's estimate of a thirty to forty five day resolution still stands, and the state's fraud investigation is still active. We'll flag it the moment there's an update. And one more date worth circling: the Planning Commission takes up the Franklin Arms rezoning on July 23rd, which would clear the way for a fifty million dollar senior housing project.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch today: the eight-thirty inflation report and Kevin Warsh's testimony right after it. If CPI lands anywhere near that three point nine percent consensus, watch how Warsh handles the obvious tension, a cooling headline number colliding with an oil shock that could reverse it by next month. His answer on that will say more about the path of rate cuts than anything he's said in his first seven weeks.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Tuesday. Have a great day.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Iran Ceasefire Crumbles, Oil Jumps, Senator Graham Dies at 71
item.description: The U.S.-Iran ceasefire collapses again as oil surges past 79 dollars a barrel and Senator Lindsey Graham dies at 71. Plus Apple sues OpenAI, mortgage rates hold near 6.5 percent, and Jacksonville catches up on the weekend.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning, and welcome back from the weekend. It's Monday, July 13th, 2026. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: We start with a ceasefire that didn't survive the weekend. The truce between the United States and Iran came apart Saturday after an attack on a container ship in the Strait of Hormuz, and by this morning, both sides had traded a fourth round of strikes in a week.

ANDREW: And closer to home, the Senate lost one of its most influential voices. Republican Lindsey Graham of South Carolina died Saturday night at 71, setting off a scramble over his seat just months before the election. We'll get to what that means.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. Heading into the weekend, the S and P 500 closed at 7,575, up about four tenths of a percent Friday. The Dow added 150 points to close near 52,637, and the Nasdaq finished higher too, near 26,282. It was the fourth winning week in five for stocks, helped along by chipmaker SK Hynix's blockbuster Wall Street debut. This morning is a different story. Stock futures are mixed, oil is jumping, and the ten-year Treasury yield is holding around 4.47 percent as investors wait on Tuesday's inflation report. The thirty-year fixed mortgage rate is tracking in the mid six percent range. We'll get into all of it.

ANDREW: Before we dive in, here's what you may have missed if you were off the grid this weekend. The Iran ceasefire fractured again, oil jumped, Senator Graham died, and a sweeping new housing law quietly took effect without the president's signature. Let's start with Iran, since that's the story shaping everything else this morning.

JENNY: Take us through what happened.

ANDREW: On Saturday, Iran's Revolutionary Guard fired on a Cyprus flagged container ship transiting the Strait of Hormuz, and Tehran declared the strait closed. The US military disputes that claim, but it responded with a new wave of strikes, hitting roughly 140 Iranian military targets. A further round followed Sunday, the fourth exchange of strikes in the span of a week, and for the first time, US forces used sea based attack drones. Iran retaliated with drone and missile attacks on US linked sites in Bahrain, Kuwait, and Jordan.

JENNY: So this is well past the pause we talked about Friday.

ANDREW: Well past it. Shipping data tracked by Bloomberg showed only a handful of vessels crossing the strait over the weekend, down from the eighteen to twenty-two ships that normally pass through each day. That's a route carrying roughly a fifth of the world's seaborne oil essentially stalled in place, and it's why oil jumped more than 4 percent this morning, with Brent crude back above 79 dollars a barrel and US crude near 74. That's still well below the peaks we saw earlier in this conflict, when Brent briefly neared 120 dollars, but it reverses weeks of gradual easing in a single weekend.

JENNY: Remind listeners why a shipping lane thousands of miles away moves prices at the pump here.

ANDREW: It comes down to concentration. A huge share of the oil that leaves the Persian Gulf, from Saudi Arabia, Iraq, the UAE, and Iran itself, has no route to open water except through that one strait. When transits drop the way they did this weekend, traders assume supply will tighten in the coming weeks even if nothing else changes, and prices move immediately on that expectation alone.

JENNY: What does the diplomatic picture look like at this point? Last week you mentioned technical talks were still happening quietly.

ANDREW: Iran's foreign minister met his Omani counterpart in Muscat over the weekend specifically to discuss safe passage through the strait, so there's still a channel open. But President Trump has said negotiating with Iran right now is, in his words, a waste of time. This is no longer a fragile pause. It's an active military exchange over a shipping lane both sides are now fighting to control.

ANDREW: The other major story from the weekend hits closer to home. Senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina died Saturday night after what his office called a brief and sudden illness. He was 71.

JENNY: What happened?

ANDREW: A preliminary medical finding points to an aortic dissection, a rupture of the aorta linked to hardening of the arteries.
